title: One project, one review, one year and a widening divide as Bill C-39 races through Parliament
content:
The president of the Nisga’a Nation told senators this week that her treaty nation backs the goal of Ottawa’s sweeping new major-projects law, even as a long line of First Nations leaders warned two parliamentary committees that 

Bill C-39

 puts deadlines ahead of constitutionally protected rights.




“The Nisga’a Nation generally supports the intent of Bill C-39 to accelerate the federal project approvals while maintaining strong environmental standards,” Eva Clayton, president of the Nisga’a Nation, told the 

Special Senate Committee on the Building Canada Strong Act on Nov. 23.




Her testimony came on the same day a special committee of MPs agreed to send the bill back to the House of Commons with amendments, according to the committee’s report.




Of the amendments the committee made to some 20 existing and new clauses, only two deal directly with Indigenous rights or consultation.




The result is a bill that has cleared the House committee largely intact, and a sharp split among First Nations over whether “one project, one review, one year” (the government’s slogan for the bill) is a path to economic reconciliation or what Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak called “a mass dilution of environmental protection and First Nation rights.”

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Plan to decolonize Manitoba’s child welfare system is a big task that will take time, says minister
content:
The director of Manitoba’s child advocacy office says that improving the current child welfare system needs a new approach that places control back to First Nations families.

However, doing so while First Nations are also struggling with a lack of resources and community spaces for the kids to thrive presents its own set of challenges.

“Decolonization is a huge undertaking,” said Sherry Gott, a member of Sapotaweyak Cree Nation who has been working in child welfare education for more than 30 years. “That means we must dismantle systems that have continued to colonize our people.”

Gott is the executive director of Manitoba’s Advocate for Children and Youth (MACY), a non-partisan social work office funded by the province. On Nov. 18, it published its latest annual report, which, among other findings, indicated that 53 per cent of serious injuries involving youth (aged 0 to 20) that resulted in a report were caused by sexual assault.

She said her “dream” would be an outcome where a typical CFS wouldn’t be necessary, because First Nations would have the resources necessary to support children who may be in crisis, but that those resources are currently hard to come by.

“We have to believe that we have the knowledge to be able to look at the system in a way where it supports our families,” Gott said. “So we also have to believe that we have traditional knowledge that is valuable. We must believe that we have the answers to support our families to thrive.”

According to the latest report from MACY, the agency doesn’t have the resources to keep up with a growing number of children in crisis.

She said the resources MACY currently needs the most is adequate staffing, and that the shortage can be “really taxing on our mental health, when you look at what comes through the door.”

“Issues of sexual exploitation and abuse is a really, really difficult subject to deal with. And when you have a name behind that incident, then you start to know who the family is and who the children are, who’s involved, it gets even more personal,” Gott continued. “Because you have names attached to it, and communities, Nations, where these children come from. So it is really hard to work daily at that level … It’s hard on our staff. But we try our best to keep their mental health and well-being in check.”

According to the report, the office received 506 referrals from April 2025 to March 2026, but only 300 were able to be reviewed, according to the legal definition of a serious injury.

Because of the demand, only 135 of the 300 referrals legally eligible for review have ended with complete serious injury reports, as of writing. Only 99 were assessed for potential investigation, and 36 of those assessments were reviewed further.

According to the 2025-2026 annual report from the office of provincial Minister of Families Nahanni Fontaine, 80 per cent of children in care are First Nations.

Similarly, Gott said that approximately 80 per cent of children represented in MACY’s serious injury reports are Indigenous.

MACY also completed 60 child death reports in 2025-26, although there were 71 in scope for a review.

Sixty-eight per cent of the children in the completed reports were Indigenous, and 98 per cent of the reports were linked to CFS.

The most recent reported death in care is five-year-old Baileigh Berens in Winnipeg. Baileigh had autism and was non-verbal, but had no known health conditions and her cause of death has not been determined. She was found in a dryer.

The Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs (AMC), which represents all 63 First Nations in Manitoba, held a sacred fire for the child at her mother’s house Wednesday evening.

Following the release of MACY’s annual report, AMC Grand Chief Kyra Wilson stated that “these findings are deeply concerning, but they are not new warnings.”

“First Nations families and survivors have been raising these concerns for decades. When children are placed in systems intended to protect them but continue to experience violence, exploitation, and abuse, we must hold those systems accountable,” she continued.

The AMC had called on Canada to examine “child welfare, child protection, and children in care” as part of the National Inquiry into Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in 2018, a recommendation that made it into the final report.

However, AMC stated, “Despite these longstanding concerns, First Nations children remain disproportionately represented in Manitoba’s child welfare system,” and that the high number of First Nations children in that system, according to the province, is “underscoring the urgent need for prevention, family reunification, and culturally appropriate supports.”

AMC, along with its own First Nations Family Advocate Office (FNFAO), stated the province would need to work “directly with First Nations governments to develop a comprehensive, culturally grounded prevention and protection strategy that addresses sexual exploitation and human trafficking, strengthens placement oversight, and ensures accessible, trauma-informed supports for children, youth, and families.”

FNFAO is a province-wide advocacy office that helps families “fighting to have their children returned to their homes or First Nations,” according to its website.

Since opening in 2015, it has worked with more than 1,500 families and has continuously urged for a total reform of the system.

According to Fontaine, changes are on the way. However, she also noted that they have taken a “very long time.”

“This is all new for everybody. But what I can tell you 100 per cent … and in five years, 10 years, and certainly in 15 years from now, child welfare will look incredibly different than it does right now. And what you will see is a system where First Nations and Métis families, leaderships, matriarchs and Elders and communities are caring collectively for children.”

Even in the last year, she said there was over a 200 per cent increase in kinship and customary care agreements, which are “voluntary, out-of-court child welfare arrangements” between the parents, the child and the respective agency.

Manitoba introduced the agreements to provincial law in 2024, to help safely keep children in their home communities without officially entering the system, Fontaine said.

“That’s phenomenal,” she said. “But what folks also have to remember is that we’re trying to decolonize a system that’s been around for 500 years, just in different forms and iterations.

“In many different iterations, Indigenous children have been harmed and have been targeted. And decolonizing these systems are going to take many, many years, but we’re doing that work right now,” Fontaine said.

In July 2026, Fontaine announced that Manitoba would conduct an independent review of its child welfare system by the end of the year, with a tentative release planned for Summer 2027. She confirmed with APTN that the process was ongoing.

“We’ve been doing all of those reviews, working with the authorities to make sure that they’re working with their agencies to ensure that children have the supports that they need,” Fontaine said. “But that work didn’t occur for many, many years. And so we’re doing that work, we’re looking at the totality of the system.”

She added that while it examines the system, the province is also working to give First Nations governments the “ability to assert jurisdiction over child welfare” when it involves their communities, and by extension, the Nation’s own laws.

“Our people are going to have a different way of doing child welfare,” Fontaine said. “It’s a way of keeping children in their communities, among their kin, among their lands, among their people. That’s something across the country that traditionally, child welfare didn’t do.”

In 2019, Ottawa passed Bill C-92, also known as an Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis Children, Youth, and Families, that, according to the government, “recognizes a simple truth: one size does not fit all when it comes to Indigenous child and family services.”

Co-developed with First Nation partners, the bill “enables Indigenous groups and communities to transition toward exercising partial or full jurisdiction over child and family services at a pace that they choose.”

While navigating the process of shifting jurisdiction in Manitoba, Fontaine acknowledged that the middle province has “the most complicated child welfare system in the country.”

Currently, child welfare in Manitoba is governed by four authorities — General Child and Family Services Authority, First Nations of Northern Manitoba Child and Family Services Authority, Southern First Nations Network of Care, and Métis Child and Family Services Authority — that oversee agencies that fall under their jurisdiction.

Although Indigenous serving authorities provide oversight and training to these agencies, it is done in accordance with provincial law and not under the jurisdiction of any specific First Nations government.

Fontaine said she’s been in care twice in her life, and although it was “needed,” she was far away from her community.

“At the end of the day, kids want to be with their family,” she said. “They want to be with their parents. They want to be with their kin. And we’re on this path to ensure that more children are staying with their family and their communities.”

However, although Gott said that Nations often have a drive to help, there is still a lack of resources.

“It’s limited, the funding that’s available,” she said. “So they make do with what they have. And when we think about things like a place for children or youth to hang out, that space needs to be safe. And it needs to have people that understand kids and where they’re coming from.

“I think it would be really important to have those in place so we’re not always responding to crisis, after crisis, after crisis,” she said.

Ultimately, Gott said, “I think what needs to be at the forefront of everybody’s mind is that children are suffering in Manitoba and I think we need to do better.”

“I hope that someday our families can go back to what they used to do, and look after our own.”

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

title: Child welfare dispute in Peguis First Nation in Manitoba sparks lockdown
content:
A dispute over the leadership and operations of Peguis First Nation’s Child and Family Services escalated Thursday with community members, the chief and a councillor gathering outside the agency’s main office.




The protest started Nov. 19 amid calls for changes to the agency’s leadership on the reserve located 200 km north of Winnipeg on the Interlake Region of Manitoba.




“Despite my attempts in the past to speak up for membership, there has been complete disregard for me as the chief of our nation, complete disregard for the concerns identified by members, and complete disregard for the safety and wellbeing of our children and our families,” Chief Stan Bird said in a video posted to social media in the days leading up to the protest.




RCMP officers arrived and spoke with the group. Bird has previously said he wants the band to take control of the CFS agency and reassert its inherent jurisdiction over child welfare.




He has also raised concerns about child safety and the agency’s operations.




Bird has not responded to further requests for comment.




Peguis CFS responded by announcing that its main office was in lockdown following Thursday’s incident.

title: Yukon to review worksheet asking students about ‘positives’ of residential school
content:
A worksheet asking high school students in Whitehorse to identify the positives of residential schools has attracted public criticism, prompting the Yukon Department of Education to commit to a curriculum review. 




A photo of the worksheet was circulated on social media late last month. The department confirmed in an email to APTN News that the worksheet was part of a Grade 10 teaching resource made available to Yukon schools in October 2024.




The person who shared the photo declined to speak with APTN, but said it came from a high school assignment at a Whitehorse school. 




The worksheet includes two experiences shared by residential school survivors whose names are blacked out. 




One question asks how some survivors, like one who attended the Carcross residential school, “insist that although there were unquestionably a lot of negative experiences at these schools, there were also many positives. What do you think were some of the positive aspects of residential school?”




Another question quotes a survivor from the Northwest Territories and asks: “To what extent do you think the positive parts of Indian residential school need to be part of what people learn about?”

author: Dennis Ward
title: Métis country singer Catie St. Germain and her journey from insecurity to the top of the charts
content:
It has only been about three years since Catie St. Germain released his first single but she has been racking up the accolades, ever since.

Growing up, St. Germain says she had a front-row seat to a legendary musician and television host, crushing it on stage every night.

Her grandfather, Ray St. Germain, is a Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame inductee, who also created and hosted a nationally syndicated variety show, Big Sky Country.

However, having a famous grandfather and a very musical family did not ensure she would follow in their footsteps.

St. Germain’s mother even tried to push her in another direction.

“She didn’t have the best experience, I think doing music. The pressure of it all was a lot for her, so, she kind of steered us away. She didn’t want her kids to have to go through the hardships of the music industry and everything,” says St. Germain on the latest episode of Face to Face.

“For a long time I just didn’t think this was something in the cards for me. But I did perform, I did sing. I joined a rock tribute band and was kind of touring with them for a while but I ended up quitting and just having kids myself and thinking it was easier and better to do the 9 to 5 thing and obviously the scheduling worked better for having kids. And then I got back to it though.

author: Fraser Needham
title: AFN calls for strengthening of First Nations Clean Water Act
content:
The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the Carney government’s proposed Bill C-37 falls short when it comes to the necessary health, legal and environmental protections to ensure access to clean drinking water.

“Clean drinking water is a human right that has been denied for generations of First Nations families across Canada,” Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said in a press release.

“Sadly, with Bill C-37, the federal government is still refusing to recognize the human right to water for First Nations in Canada.”

Woodhouse Nepinak was a witness before the Indigenous and Northern Affairs Committee on Tuesday, which is studying the proposed legislation.

The AFN says Bill C-37, also known as the First Nations Clean Water Act, is significantly weaker than legislation drafted by the previous Trudeau government.

Bill C-61, which did not pass because Parliament was prorogued under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, recognized First Nations access to clean drinking water as a human right, but has been weakened under the current legislation to the “progressive realization.”

It took Carney more than a year to reintroduce the new legislation.

content:
Nunavut’s child advocate says information presented to the territory’s legislature by the minister of Family Services regarding child welfare issues was “absolutely, patently untrue.” 




Jane Bates, the Representative for Children and Youth Nunavut, told APTN News that Gwen Healy Akearok has on multiple occasions made false statements to the territorial legislature. 

 




According to Bates, in a May 22 statement, Akearok said her department had “completed a full update of our standards and procedures manual, which now reflects best practices in social work with a priority focus on Inuit culture and maintaining connection to family.”




Bates said she was astonished to hear this announcement.







“I was listening to it thinking, ‘What? Hang on here,’” she said. “So I went back to them and I said, ‘You don’t have any section for children in care and you have no section for foster care. How is it that you’ve got a comprehensive standards and procedures manual?’”

title: APTN and Sportsnet to feature 6 NHL games in Plains Cree, Inuktitut
content:
APTN and Rogers Sportsnet announced that six NHL games will be broadcast in Plains Cree and Inuktitut this season.




The games will air on APTN’s regular network along with its APTN Languages channel.




All the games are on Saturday evening, with the first on Nov. 28 that will feature a game between Gavin McKenna and the Toronto Maple Leafs and Pittsburgh Penguins.




The statement said the first three broadcasts will be presented in Plains Cree, followed by three in Inuktitut. All games will air live and run until April 10.




“This hockey season, APTN delivers a hat trick: exciting game action, opportunities to reclaim Indigenous languages and stronger connections to our communities through the power of sport. Hearing a game called in your language helps keep it part of everyday life, while welcoming fans of every background to share in the experience,” said Mike Omelus, APTN executive director of Content and Programming Strategy, in a 

statement on Tuesday. 




“Thanks to our partnership with Rogers and Sportsnet, we’re proud to continue creating space for Indigenous languages to thrive on one of the country’s biggest stages.”

title: Regional leaders say future of Aurora College campuses remains unclear
content:
For the last two years, Dana Fergusson has been asking Aurora College the same questions.




As chair of Thebacha Leadership Council, she wants to know what academic programs will be offered at the college’s Fort Smith and Inuvik campuses as the institution works toward becoming a polytechnic university.




She also wants to know how decisions about program locations are being made, what progress the college has made toward its transformation and how much the process has cost.




“Where are the measurable outcomes on where they are with getting closer to this polytech?” Fergusson said in an interview with APTN News. “And then tell me where the money went.”




The Thebacha Leadership Council is governed by local leadership from Salt River First Nation, Tthebatthie Denesuline Nation, Fort Smith Métis Council and Town of Fort Smith.




On Nov. 18, the council sent a second open letter to Aurora College’s board of governors, the minister of Education, Culture and Employment and all members of the legislative assembly.




The letter asks the college to make clear commitments on regional program delivery, including transparent criteria for deciding where programs are offered, an assessment of campus infrastructure and utilization, and in-person engagement with communities.

title: Letters from 1914 reveal worry that Shoal Lake water rights would cripple Winnipeg aqueduct
content:
A century-old exchange of letters between senior government officials is at the heart of a $2 billion lawsuit alleging Indigenous water rights were sacrificed to ensure Winnipeg could draw its drinking water from 

Shoal Lake

.




In 1914, Ontario deputy minister of lands, forests and mines Aubrey White warned federal Indian Affairs deputy superintendent general Duncan Campbell Scott that honouring existing legislative commitments to First Nations could “cripple” Winnipeg’s proposed aqueduct project.




The letters were uncovered by a historian hired by lawyer Julian Falconer’s firm.




“Completely out of sight of the First Nations, completely in secret, the deputy minister in a letter that we now have, says, if we follow through on this it would cripple, and that’s the word he used, cripple the Winnipeg water project,” says Falconer.




Falconer’s firm is representing Iskatewizaagegan (Shoal Lake) No. 39 Independent First Nation in litigation heading to trial against the City of Winnipeg and Ontario.




A statement of claim filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in 2024, alleges ecological, cultural and financial impacts resulting from Winnipeg’s aqueduct intake in Shoal Lake and seeks $2 billion in damages.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Canada begins recruiting commissioners to review possible wrongful convictions
content:
Nearly two years after it was first announced, the 

federal government

 has begun recruiting commissioners for a new independent body that will look at potential wrongful convictions, a key step toward replacing the current ministerial review process.




Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced Monday that the Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission will operate independently of government, police, prosecutors and the courts. The commission will investigate applications from people who say they were wrongly convicted and decide whether cases should be returned to court.




“Wrongful convictions can have lasting consequences. We’re taking the next step in establishing a commission that will review these cases independently of government,” Fraser said in a news release. “Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to court to consider new information.”




Parliament passed the Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission Act, also known as David and Joyce Milgaard’s Law, Dec. 17, 2024. The law permits the creation of the commission to replace the existing ministerial review system.

content:

Selon des habitués du secteur et des intervenants de rue œuvrant auprès des personnes en situation d’itinérance dans l’ouest du centre-ville, les rapports entre la police et les personnes itinérantes au square Cabot et dans les environs sont marqués par la méfiance et la peur.




Au cours d’une période de deux semaines, les personnes interrogées par APTN Nouvelles au square Cabot ont affirmé avoir reçu de nombreuses contraventions, représentant des centaines de dollars d’amende, pour non-paiement du titre de transport ou pour avoir traversé la rue Sainte-Catherine hors des intersections autorisées. Des personnes buvant de l’alcool dans le square ont aussi rapporté avoir reçu des amendes pour possession de contenants ouverts. Bien peu cherchent à payer leurs contraventions. Pour eux, en recevoir une nouvelle fait tout simplement partie de la réalité au square Cabot, bien que cela puisse éventuellement fournir à la police un prétexte pour les arrêter.

title: Yukon court dismisses wrongful death lawsuit against Whitehorse shelter operator
content:
The Supreme Court of Yukon has dismissed a wrongful death lawsuit against the operator of the Whitehorse emergency shelter.

Chief Justice Suzanne Duncan said in a Nov. 6 decision that the lawsuit was brought after the one-year limitation period under the Yukon’s Fatal Accidents Act.

title: Outgoing Green Party leader says Carney is the most ‘opaque, unaccountable person in politics’
content:
Elizabeth May says Prime Minister Mark Carney is perhaps the most challenging party leader she has had to work with in more than four decades in politics.




“Accountability is really important and Mr. Carney is the most opaque, unaccountable person in politics I think I have ever seen,” the Green Party MP said.




May stepped down as Green Party leader earlier this month, making way for former Kitchener, Ontario MP Mike Morrice to take over the party’s reins.




She will continue on as the MP for the riding of Saanich-Gulf Islands in British Columbia.




One of the reasons May voted in favour of the 2025 budget was Carney’s pledge to respect Canada’s Paris commitments on climate change.

title: Nunavut child advocate considered suing territorial government over child welfare stonewalling
content:
Nunavut’s child advocate says she was ready to take the territory’s Department of Family Services to court because of what she characterized as the DFS stonewalling her office’s access to information pertaining to Nunavummiut children in care. 




Jane Bates told Nunavut’s legislative assembly in September that despite an information-sharing protocol, the department was deciding for itself whether, and when, her office should be involved in assessing its conduct.




“This situation has become so serious,” the Representative for Children and Youth (RCYO) told legislators, “that earlier this year I advised the deputy minister that, unless the underlying issue concerning the RCYO’s statutory authority and the department’s corresponding obligations could be resolved, I was prepared to withdraw from the GN–RCYO Protocol and seek the assistance of the Nunavut Court of Justice to ensure that our office could carry out its statutory mandate.







“If significant limits, safeguards and independent oversight are not put in place, the department will continue to operate in the same manner with the same results.”

title: Top court won’t hear bid for class-action lawsuit on behalf of Indigenous children
content:
The Supreme of Court of Canada will not hear a bid to certify a class-action lawsuit against Ottawa on behalf of Indigenous children who were taken from their families while living away from reserves and placed in non-Indigenous care.




The class-action claim is based on Canada’s duty to protect Indigenous children in care from harm, specifically as it relates to the loss of their identity.




The lawsuit challenges Canada’s role between Jan. 1, 1992 and Dec. 31, 2019 in allowing Indigenous children in state care to be placed in non-Indigenous homes.




In 2022, the Federal Court ruled the matter could go ahead as a class action for those affected in all provinces and territories.




Last year, the Federal Court of Appeal overturned that decision, saying Canada does not have possession, power or control over documents and information relevant to the claim.




The Court of Appeal also said the preferable course would be proceedings before courts that can compel the participation of provinces responsible for administration and delivery of child and family services to off-reserve Indigenous children.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Manitoba group needs $17M to bring 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home
content:
A Manitoba-based organization is trying to raise $17 million to bring 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home from Switzerland.

“It doesn’t matter what tribe you’re from, it’s important that our people come together to bring these home to our Nations,” said Karl Stone, spiritual advisor of the group Return the Sacred. “And have these stored in a place where they can be kept for our own medicine people, within our own communities.

Return the Sacred, formerly called the Bringing Them Home Project, is a grassroots organization formed in 2025.

“That’s the way these sacred bundles should be taken care of, I believe. And these sacred bundles should be taught to the next generation.”

The group, headed by executive director Coleen Rajotte, returned from a week-long trip to Switzerland Thursday and held a news conference in Winnipeg.

Since June 2025, the group has been in communication with a private collector, Vincent Escriba, who ran the Indian Land Museum in Gossau, Switzerland.

The museum contained over 5,000 artefacts from North and South America, as well as several countries in Africa. They’re all part of Escriba’s private collection, which he has been growing for the majority of his adult life.

“He is actually a kind, gentle person,” Rajotte said. “He became enamoured with Indigenous people and Indigenous culture.”

She said he “spent his entire life travelling to North America,” 50 trips overall, collecting the items and purchasing other private collections in full.

“That’s how he’s collected such a vast quality,” she said. “We do believe him that he wants to work with us,” she said. “He’s now 70 years old, he’s put all his energy and all his money into this collection, and now he wants to sell it back.”

The Indian Land Museum closed in December 2025, when Escriba decided to retire. Since then, the artefacts have been stored in boxes in a private warehouse, awaiting sale.

Prior to its closure, the chief of Pikangikum First Nation, a community located in northern Ontario, had been advised of the collection’s fate. The chief told Gerald Neufeld, a long-time researcher based in Winnipeg, who created the group in an effort to bring the artefacts home.

The collection includes headdresses, unopened medicine bags, medicine and corn husk masks, pipes, totem poles, canoes, and several other types of artefacts that carry spiritual and cultural weight, Rajotte said.

Escriba also owns several boxes of textbooks, both in English and German.

Over several days, the group met with Escriba and took hundreds of photos of descriptions, contained in stacks of binders, which identified each object, along with its origin, in German.

They have not been able to confirm when all of the artefacts were made, but estimate most left Canada between 1840 and 1860.

Similarly, Rajotte said she is still working to figure out what came from where, but has so far been able to confirm several objects were from Nations in southern Alberta and North Dakota.

They also negotiated with Escriba and determined how much it would cost to purchase the items and return them to North America: $14.5 million, as well as an additional $3 million to cover transportation and handling of the items.

“Of course, there’s lots of opinions,” Rajotte said about Escriba’s decision to sell, rather than donate, the items back to the Nations they originally came from.

In California, she continued, the California Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act requires that all state-funded agencies, museums and universities must return any Indigenous cultural items, without a cost, by law.

However, even if the same laws existed in Canada, the situation with Escriba would be different, Rajotte said, due to his collection being private.

She said they are planning to negotiate with Escriba about lowering the price, or a long-term payment plan, but she doesn’t believe he’ll budge when it comes to the bill.

However, he has extended the sale’s deadline, which was originally set for payment by the end of December 2026.

Rajotte said she predicts it will take “at least” a year to appraise, document and pay for the entire collection.

So far, Heritage Canada has covered the initial trip to Switzerland, but there have been no additional conversations with public or private funders regarding the price of the collection itself.

“Our peoples’ sacred belongings that are in museums all over the world should be returned to the original people of this true land,” Stone said. “The bundles need to be protected … need to be cared for in a sacred way.”

Rajotte said, additionally, items are seen as living relatives, “ and the fact that they’re in a warehouse right now … no one’s spending time with them, visiting with them, makes me very very sad.”

She said her “biggest fear” was running out of time and not being able to purchase the collection, and that it will then be sold to private buyers and live out the rest of their days in office buildings in Dubai or New York City.

Stone said “it’s out of [his] hands,” but that he prays “that the right thing is done.

“It’s up to him [Escriba], but in our culture, we don’t believe there’s a price tag on anything that is sacred,” he said. “It’s sacred to us, that’s our way of life, that’s our culture, our belief, and hopefully something good will come of this.”

Return the Sacred will be hosting a fundraiser on Dec. 3. Money from the first event will go towards creating a digital archive and hiring a larger team.

The group’s short-term plan will be to translate each artefact description from German to English, with the use of artificial intelligence and a translator to double-check, to determine which artefact belongs to who.

Rajotte is encouraging “anyone with deep pockets” to reach out to the organization and donate to the cause.

“We’re working really hard to make sure we get all these items back to Turtle Island where they belong,” she said.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: First Nations Leadership Council sends open letter to the prime minister, Indigenous Services over delay in passing Bill S-2
content:
In an open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull Masty, the First Nations Leadership Council (FNLC) is calling for an immediate end to the second-generation cut-off.

The FNLC is made up of the B.C. Assembly of First Nations, First Nations Summit and the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs. It’s calling for an end to sex and race-based discrimination in the Indian Act, and removal of the second-generation cutoff.

“We fully support the amendments to Bill S-2 made by the Standing Senate Committee on Indigenous Peoples and adopted by the Senate of Canada on December 4, 2025,” the FNLC said in the letter.

“Further, we are concerned with the Minister of Indigenous Services Canada’s (ISC) use of a secretive process regarding the new standalone legislation, which violates the legal duty to consult in good faith.”

The second-generation cutoff is when a person, under section 6(1) of the Indian Act, passes status to a child no matter who the other parent is. But a person under section 6(2) can pass it on only if the other parent is also registered as “status” under the Indian Act.

After two generations of parenting with someone who is not registered, the third generation is out. That is the second-generation cut-off.

The FNLC maintains that the immediate elimination of the second-generation cut-off is supported by UN human rights bodies including the UN Human Rights Committee, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women, and, in May 2026, the UN Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

“For months, Bill S-2 has been stalled in the Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs (INAN Committee), while the Minister insisted upon further consultations and then argued for broader registration reform and confused the issues of band membership and self-determination over citizenship with Indian status, and is now proposing new draft legislation. These deceptive tactics are a red herring to distract and delay the passage of Bill S-2,” the letter stated.

First Nations Summit Political executive Robert Phillips said in an interview with APTN News that it’s frustrating that “we’ve governed ourselves for thousands of years. And to remove second-generation cutoff and maybe replace it with universal one parent rule, or introducing legislation-and then it’s stalling?”

“We’re getting to the point where now we’re in argumentative stage…I do believe we need to be at a table and say that the authority should rest with First Nations and those that have treaties or those that have Aboriginal rights like here in British Columbia…,” Phillips said.

According to Phillips, Gull-Masty has invited “select First Nations leaders” to consult with ISC on new draft legislation to address the second-generation cut-off.

In the letter to Carney and Gull-Masty, the FNLC said, “we understand that… the minister has invited select First Nations leaders to consult with ISC regarding new draft legislation to address the second-generation cut-off, on the condition that they sign a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA), which binds them to not disclose any information that is shared with them for a period of five years, unless that information is disclosed to the public by the Minister.”

That doesn’t sit well with the FNLC.

“Using NDAs to convene meetings with selected leaders blocks First Nations leaders from consulting their Nations, members, technical and legal advisors. This secretive and selective process is an alarming escalation of the government’s tactics to undermine the broad support of First Nations.”

Senators vote to end the second-generation cutoff for ‘status Indians’

According to a statement from Gull-Masty’s office, a “collaborative process” on the second-generation cut off and section 10 voting thresholds concluded at the end of July, where the government invited First Nations to “put forward their own proposals and solutions to address these inequities in the Indian Act.

“We heard a range of perspectives, proposals, and priorities, alongside a shared sense of urgency: the second generation cut-off must be addressed,” according to a statement provided by Gull-Masty’s office. “While the Collaborative Process has now concluded, the work continues. We are currently reviewing the proposals, feedback and perspectives shared through the process to inform next steps, including legislative reform.”

The FNLC said the process goes against “the vast majority of First Nations across Canada” and introducing new standalone legislation ignores “broad support from First Nations and First Nations rights-holders…and directly contravenes the mandate of the vast majority of First Nations across Canada, who are on record supporting the immediate passage of Bill S-2 as amended by the Senate.”

title: ISC minister says she was not expecting Kinew’s comments about abolishing the Indian Act
content:
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty says she was as surprised as anyone when Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew raised the idea of abolishing the Indian Act last month and was hoping for more information on what role the province would play.

“I think it’s interesting to see somebody who’s a provincial premier wanting to frame up that space,” she said. “Clearly, in his role he would have to indicate his responsibility in the provincial seat and how you would serve those off-reserve community members.

“I think that’s the initiative I was hoping to see as a minister coming out of that space because you have to increase the responsibility, the partnership, the role of the provincial government in the path beyond the Indian Act.”

The idea of getting rid of the Indian Act was raised by Kinew during a press conference at the First Nations First Ministers meeting in Ottawa on Oct. 26.

Hand-drummers from the Ottawa River Singers opened the demonstration.

content:

content:

title: Grieving mother livestreams private Manitoba police watchdog meeting to force transparency
content:
A grieving mother is taking transparency into her own hands by livestreaming meetings with Manitoba’s police watchdog and justice minister over the lack of independent investigation into her daughter’s violent arrest and subsequent death.




Crystal Delvenne said she chose to livestream the meetings to Facebook because she’s “lost trust in these systems” over the last few months following the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba’s (IIU) refusal to investigate an arrest by the Brandon Police Service (BPS).




Crystal’s daughter Cassity told her police beat her during the June 12 arrest, leaving her with bruised ribs, bleeding ears and hearing loss.




Cassity was found dead in her apartment of an unknown cause nine days later. Police said Cassity’s death is unrelated to her arrest.




On Friday, BPS announced it concluded its investigation into her death, saying a “definitive cause of death has been determined,” but added it could not share it publicly due to privacy laws and out of respect for the family.




According to the family, nothing has been received at the time this story was published.

title: InFocus: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s declaration on abolishing the Indian Act an ‘absurd distraction’
content:
At the noon break at the First Nations First Ministers Meeting in Ottawa, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew quoted to Karl Marx as he forwarded his call to action.




“Abolish the 

Indian Act

,” Kinew said. “You have nothing to lose but your chains.”




This week on APTN News InFocus, our guests Pam Palmater and Veldon Coburn argue First Nations have much to lose.




“There are thousands of bylaws and codes, and other laws that First Nations have passed to govern their communities under the Indian Act that have to be addressed,” said Palmater, a lawyer and chair in Indigenous Governance at Toronto Metropolitan University. “All of these things are constitutionally protected.




“So, you literally cannot say, ‘Hey, let’s just abolish it’. That alone, dealing with that intricate web of laws and constitutional issues, that’s going to take a long, long time.”




Canadian leaders have been toying with abolishing or amending the Indian Act for more than 70 years.




As Palmater notes, there’s a pattern.




“During the 1969 White Paper, you had [former prime minister] Pierre Elliot Trudeau who wanted to make Canada self-sufficient in oil and gas. That was his big agenda item,” Palmater said. “All of a sudden, well, Treaty rights might stand in the way, and First Nations, so let’s get rid of the Indian Act.”

title: Manitoba Métis Federation ‘appalled’ by being left out of budget
content:
The Manitoba Métis Federation (MMF) says it’s “appalled” that it was left out of the federal budget.




“In recent years, Canada has finally started to address the long-overlooked needs of the Red River Métis in areas such as housing, early learning and childcare, and post-secondary education,” said David Chartrand, president of the MMF, 

in a statement released Friday. 




“However, a significant gap still exists between our Nation and the general population. There’s no doubt our people will be angered that their needs have been dismissed by this Budget.”




On Thursday, the federal government tabled a budget with $50 billion worth of promises, mainly for First Nations housing and infrastructure. For Inuit, the budget renewed the Inuit Child First Initiative / Piratsiagutiit at $575 million over five years, and the government is also putting $610 million over four years for the Nutrition North subsidy.




Métis are only found once in the 532 page budget document, “as part of the title for a piece of legislation, 

An Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families 

– a piece of legislation that Canada has claimed they do not have a mechanism to fund us for.”

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Indian Act controversy lingers more than a week after abolishment was raised in Ottawa
content:
Everyone, from pundits, constitutional lawyers and scholars to people in coffee shops and online, has been hashing out just what it could mean to abolish the Indian Act after it was raised by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew on Oct. 26 in Ottawa.




However, Kinew hasn’t provided context for his comment, which came out at what was the first First Nations First Ministers meeting in decades and touched off a firestorm of debate over what doing away with the controversial Act would actually do.




APTN News has reached out to Kinew’s office and requested an interview on several occasions, but those requests have been denied.




“We just had one of the most impactful meetings of the decade in Ottawa and everyone on social media is talking about the Indian Act and the complexities of whether or not it can be abolished and the problems if it is and all these different things, said Jennifer Laewetz, the CEO of Paskwâw Strategies, an Indigenous advisory firm in Saskatchewan. “It’s a little bit frustrating because we need to be united on a lot of other bigger issues right now.”




“I just really wish that our leaders would recognize sometimes that they have so much impact in these spaces that if you are going to say something as big as ‘you need to abolish the Indian Act’ you need to be prepared to follow up with people in Canada about what that looks like… and communicate how you see tha

author: Fraser Needham
title: Algonquin activist says Carney government needs more focus on climate change initiatives
content:
An Algonquin environmental activist says the Carney government’s priorities are misplaced when it comes to climate change initiatives.




“Essentially in 2025, the budget committed $81.8 billion in increased military spending over five years and so that’s telling us that while they may be making these commitments for environmental protection for workers and jobs – at the end of the day they’re still heavily interested in the global military complex which is one of the main drivers of climate change,” Dara Wawatie-Chabot said on the latest episode of Nation to Nation.




“Their commitments are just not meeting the demands that they are actually committing to in these budgets.”




Earlier in the week, a group called the Youth Climate Corps held a news conference in Ottawa calling on the Liberal government to do more when it comes to climate change.




The organization says the 2025 budget put $40 million toward a Youth Climate Corps pilot program but a year later it has yet to be launched.




They are also calling for a further $1 billion to be invested in green jobs for young people.

title: Budget 2026 commits $32B to First Nations housing, infrastructure while leaving most Métis, Inuit pre-budget asks unaddressed
content:
The federal government’s 2026 budget pledges more than $32 billion over 10 years for First Nations housing and infrastructure on reserve, calling the investment a shift toward “greater certainty and stability for long-term planning.”




The spending plan, released Thursday under the chapter “Advancing reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples,” states that “every person living in Canada should have access to clean and safe drinking water, adequate housing, and dependable infrastructure, but for too many First Nations communities, clean water remains out of reach.”




It positions the new funding as essential “to supporting healthy communities, a good quality of life, and economic opportunities.”




The core commitment




According to the budget, the government will launch a First Nations On-Reserve Infrastructure Program with $18.5 billion over 10 years starting in 2027-28.




The document says this funding “will support the construction and maintenance of a broad range of assets, from roads and bridges to schools and health facilities, while extending investments in water and wastewater infrastructure for six years beyond funding announced in June 2026.”




On housing, Budget 2026 proposes $11 billion over 10 years “to improve First Nations housing” and an additional $1.7 billion over five years “to accelerate housing construction.”

author: Emma Honeybun
title: ‘The grift stops now’: Democratic midterm elections sweep brings in first Indigenous governor and senator in U.S. history
content:
The 2026 U.S. midterms resulted in several firsts, including the victories of Peggy Flanagan and Deb Haaland, the first Indigenous women to serve as state senator and governor, respectively, in the country’s history.




“My ancestors came to the Rio Grande Valley in the late 1200s, and this beautiful land has sustained all of us for generations,” Haaland said in her victory speech Tuesday night. “Just off this road, my grandmother was taken to boarding school, and along with my grandfather, survived through a time when the federal government attempted to strip them of their languages, traditions and identities. Yet, we are still here.”




Although the results have not been finalized, the Democrats have been favoured to win the U.S. House of Representatives (236 seats to 129) and Senate (54 to 44), a sweeping result which flipped 29 seats from red to blue, as of Wednesday afternoon.




Midterm elections are held two years after a presidential election. All members of Congress, also called the House of Representatives, are up for election, and 33 of the Senate’s 100 seats were up for grabs.




Alongside Flanagan (Minnesota) and Haaland (New Mexico), the midterms also brought in Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator in Michigan; Chris Pappas, the first openly gay senator in New Hampshire; and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in Georgia.

content:
It has been five months since a judge issued a court order requiring the Assembly of First Nations and the other parties named in a lawsuit by former national chief RoseAnne Archibald to produce their documents by July 31.

Nearly three months later, Archibald’s lawyer says they’re still waiting.

David Shiller said the AFN and the other parties remain in breach of that order, forcing the matter back before the court for another case conference and another delay.

“Oral examination for discovery (was to) occur, between November second and November 9th,” Shiller said in an interview with APTN News. He added that they’ve still not received the required documents. On July 31, 2026, what they delivered to me was what they called a draft affidavit of documents, and it was only purporting to be from the AFN.

“There was nothing delivered on behalf of the individual defendants who were the individual members of the executive committee.”

title: Mississaugas of the Credit invests $15M million to become shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada
content:
Mississaugas of the Credit in Ontario has invested $15 million in First Nations Bank of Canada, becoming one of the bank’s largest shareholders with an ownership stake of approximately 10 per cent.

The $15-million dollar investment for an approximate 10 per cent stake values First Nation Bank of Canada at roughly $150 million

The deal, announced Wednesday at Canadian Club in Toronto, completes a $50 million capital raise by the bank and brings the total number of First Nations and shareholders to 117.

Chief Margaret Sault said the investment is part of the Nation’s long-term economic strategy.

“This investment represents an important step forward in our Nation’s commitment to building a strong and sustainable economic future for our people,” Sault said. “By becoming a major shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada, we are investing in an opportunity to build long-term wealth for our community with a partner who understands our needs and aspirations.

“Meaningful participation in the Canadian economy includes having ownership in the institutions that help drive and shape its future. We see this investment as an opportunity to create lasting benefits for future generations,” she added.

author: Dennis Ward
title: SCO grand chief given a ‘reprieve’ from a vote that could have ousted him
content:
The grand chief of an organization that represents 33 Anishinaabe and Dakota Nations in southern Manitoba will carry on in his leadership role until at least June 2027.

This past summer, a former ally of Jerry Daniels brought forward a motion seeking a vote to remove him as leader of the Southern Chiefs Organization (SCO).

“Chiefs have raised numerous concerns regarding governance, leadership, accountability, transparency, organization decision-making and the confidence of member Nations in the current leadership of the Organization,” said a resolution at the time tabled by Lake Manitoba Chief Cornell McLean.

A response, at the time, attributed to the SCO Chiefs Executive Committee, cited the financial cost of a summit, among other reasons, and called for the motion to be brought forward at an ordinary summit

That meeting, SCO’s Chiefs-in-Summit gathering, got underway on Wednesday in Brokenhead Ojibway Nation, where a vote on Daniels’ leadership was expected.

According to an SCO spokesperson, “the Chiefs withdrew the proposed non-confidence motion at today’s SCO Chiefs-in-Summit, and no vote was held.”

McLean told APTN News that “it wasn’t a win for him, it’s more like a reprieve. We decided to wait until his term is over in June.”

title: Air Creebec hit by administrative data breach affecting employees and passengers
content:
Air Creebec, a regional Quebec airline owned by the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee, reported a data breach Wednesday affecting both customers and staff.

In a press release, the company announced “an unauthorized intrusion targeting some of its administrative systems.”

The release stresses that the breach did not compromise any systems associated with aircraft, flight operations or flight safety, noting the company’s administrative systems were not connected with aircraft and flight systems, which it said operate independently.

“Initial findings indicate that administrative files were exfiltrated,” states the release. “These files may contain personal information relating mainly to current and former employees, as well as passengers. Others may also contain operational, administrative or financial information related to customers and partners. The review is ongoing.”

Based in the airport of Val d’Or in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region of western Quebec, roughly 520 kilometres northwest of Ottawa, Air Creebec offers flights to 16 destinations in Quebec and Ontario. The company’s fleet consists of 21 Dash-8 turboprop regional airliners, along with one ATR 72 turboprop air-freighter for cargo, and carries 200,000 passengers per year.

title: Two years after Joshua Papigatuk died in a police shooting, Salluit awaits answers
content:
Two years after a police intervention in Salluit ended with Joshua Papigatuk dead and his twin brother Garnet Papigatuk seriously injured, Quebec prosecutors have decided whether the officers involved will face criminal charges but are waiting to speak to the family before making their decision public.




Lucas Bastien, spokesperson for the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions, said an announcement is expected soon but did not specify when.




“Our decision to proceed or not can only be made public once we have met with the deceased’s family,” he said in an email Tuesday to Nunatsiaq News.




Early on Nov. 4, 2024, 

two police officers responded to a report

 of impaired driving, according to a news release from Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes, Quebec’s police watchdog, at the time of the incident.




Minutes later, an altercation broke out between the officers and two people. Police used a stun gun and pepper spray to try to control them.




An officer fired a gun once in the direction of one of the individuals, who was injured. A struggle continued with the second person and more shots were fired. One was pronounced dead, and the other was medevaced.

content:
For the first time, 10-year-old Kenna back-weaves the threads of a beaded loom belt that she designed and beaded herself.




Glossy white beads cover the loom as bright and colourful designs, a turtle to represent the turtle clan; her favourite flowers, roses and forget-me-nots; and a monarch butterfly–her favourite insect- fill the belt.




Kenna sits in a large leather-cushioned chair, leaning over the loom. After she’s beaded one row, she highlights the section of her design on a printed-out drawing of the loom belt, keeping track of each row she’s completed.




As she focuses on weaving each bead through the loom, her mother, Kelly Back, stands beside her, guiding her through the process.




“Then you pull it through,” says Kelly, watching over her daughter. “There you go.”

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: AFN presses Ottawa for funded plan to close $376B infrastructure gap in upcoming federal budget
content:
The Assembly of First Nations is calling on the federal government to use Thursday’s budget to set out a fully funded plan, developed with First Nations, to close an infrastructure gap now estimated at more than $376 billion.

National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said at a news conference Tuesday that the scale of the infrastructure gap shortfall demands immediate and sustained attention.

“The AFN estimates put the First Nations infrastructure gap at over $376 billion over the next ten years. Canada committed to closing this gap by 2030. The budget must set out a funded plan with First Nations to deliver on that commitment,” she said.

Woodhouse Nepinak pointed to joint research with the Conference Board of Canada showing the economic payoff of those investments.

“Through our research with the Conference Board of Canada, the Assembly of First Nations describes how these generational investments will create hundreds of thousands of jobs and return $1.82 for every one dollar invested in closing the gap,” she said.

She warned that continued underfunding is driving costs higher.

“Federal investment has not kept pace with First Nations infrastructure needs, and delays are making the gap more costly to close.”

The national chief noted that Prime Minister Mark Carney has already acknowledged more is required.

author: Dennis Ward
title: Inuk actress Anna Lambe says North of North role has brought ‘so much joy into her life’
content:
Inuk actress Anna Lambe was willing to do anything to score a role, any role, on 

North of North

.




Lambe had auditioned for the lead role of Siaja but was losing sleep as time passed and she hadn’t received a call back.




Lambe had previously worked with the creators, Stacey Aglok MacDonald and Alethea Arnaquq-Baril on the critically acclaimed film 

The Grizzlies 

and knew from the outset that 

North of North 

was going to be great.




“I didn’t expect that it was going to be this big because the writing was there, the team was there, the casting was there, everything was there to make this show a hit show,” says Lambe on the latest episode of 

Face to Face

. “It had all of the elements to make it very, very good. So, from the moment I read the breakdown, I was like yup this is the stuff. This is what the kids call the stuff.




“While we were shooting, I had no fears. I had fears about my performance, it was my first time doing comedy, so I was terrified and I would look up at the ceiling going to bed going alright that was my last day on set, I’m going to get fired tomorrow, they’re going to have a new Saija and that’s ok.




“That didn’t happen but the actual content of the show, I was like people are going to love this, I love this, we all love this, we all love making it.”




The first season of North of North was nominated for 20 Canadian Screen Awards.

content:

“When children are removed from their homes and placed in foster care for their protection, the department takes on responsibility for their safety and well-being,” the auditor general’s team writes in the introduction to the report. “Yet, the department [of Family Services] still could not consistently demonstrate that the basic safeguards intended to protect those children were being followed.”

This year’s audit is focused on foster care and finds there have been little to no changes to serious flaws in the system that the auditor general previously identified and marked for attention.

content:

title: Cody Drygeese makes history as Yellowknife swears in new mayor and council
content:
Cody Drygeese held his drum as he swore to serve the city of Yellowknife for the next four years. It was a proud moment with family in attendance, including both of his grandmothers.




The newly elected councillor is a member of the Yellowknives Dene First Nation, and is believed to be the first person from the First Nation elected to the position.




“I asked if I could swear my oath of office over my drum and they said okay,” Drygeese told 

APTN News

 following Monday’s ceremony.




Drygeese received 3,439 votes in the Oct. 19 municipal election, more than any other council candidate. He was one of eight councillors sworn in alongside newly elected Mayor Melissa Syer on Nov. 2, 2026.




Drygeese said he never felt the need to put on a facade during his campaign and doesn’t plan to change who he is now that he has taken office.




“I didn’t make any false promises. I didn’t put on a politician’s face and say, vote for me,” he said. “I was just myself this entire time and I was participating in my culture and I was sharing my culture and our ceremonies with everybody.”

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: St’át’imc Chiefs Council challenges Ottawa’s pipeline plans in court
content:
A group of First Nations in British Columbia announced they have filed a federal court application for a judicial review of the federal government’s decision to fast-track the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline between Alberta and BC as a “project of national interest.” In a press conference held in Richmond B.C. this morning, members of the St’át’imc Chiefs Council — representing eleven Nations of the St’át’imc people (also known as Lilloee) —decried what they called a lack of consultation and stressed the need for the courts to slow the developmental process.

Chief Bonnie Adolph of the Sekw’el’was (Cayoose Creek) First Nation began by outlining threats to the salmon upon which her people rely. She said that when her community wrote to the Major Projects Office asking to be consulted about listing the project under the Build Canada Act, they were told since their land was not on the proposed pipeline route, the Crown would not consult with them.

“When we told the Major Projects Office their narrow geographic approach failed to account for downstream, interconnected and cumulative environmental risks to our inherent St’át’imc title and rights,” Adolph said, “We were told that we could send comments like any member of the public, but not as a First Nation whom the Crown had a legal [duty] to consult. author: The Canadian Press
title: Difficult and unpopular decisions ahead, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says
content:
British Columbia premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said the Conservative caucus of 63 legislators is united to lead the province but he also warned of difficult and unpopular decisions ahead.







Doerkson made the comments as newly elected Conservatives gathered for their first caucus meeting on Monday, where he told them that their job now is to govern on behalf of all constituents, no matter which party people voted for in the Oct. 24 election.




He said Conservatives owe every British Columbian the same effort and respect.




“That is the responsibility, of course, that comes from winning, but it makes making difficult decisions somewhat, maybe unpopular.”




He said that B.C. residents don’t expect perfection, but they do want honesty, effort and integrity from their government, and elected Conservatives must put the public ahead of their own party’s interests every single time.




Doerkson said people will be watching to see if his caucus will splinter as it did under the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.




“I know that there will be a lot of commentary about this caucus, and a lot of people watching to see whether or not we can hold it together,” he said.




“So, let me save everyone the suspense: this caucus is unified,” Doerkson said to cheers from the crowd.

title: Feds declare Roberts Bank 2 expansion ‘project of national interest’
content:
A large-scale port expansion to be located off the coast of Delta, B.C., has been labelled as a ‘project of national interest,’ a designation which, according to environmental advocates, could result in the extinction of the Southern Resident Killer Whales.

title: Family of Miranda Mamakwa seeking criminal investigation into ‘negligent’ death of mother
content:
The family of a woman who died after a federal program did not arrange transportation to medical appointments is asking for a criminal investigation.

“The criminal justice system should only be invoked where grounds exist to believe a crime has been committed,” read the statement from the family. “Public officials are as accountable as anyone else in this country for reckless acts that endanger those in their charge.”

According to her family, Miranda Mamakwa died on Sept. 8 after she didn’t receive transportation to multiple important appointments following an open-heart surgery.

She was 31 and the mother of three kids.

“Literally, the blood of Indigenous people is required for any kind of meaningful change,” said Julian Falconer, legal counsel for the family. “We have created a pattern of behavior where we only get their attention once they [Canada] have killed somebody.”

Mamakwa was a member of Fort Severn First Nation, the northernmost community in Ontario, and was relying on transportation from the Non-Insured Health Benefits Program (NIHB) to get to follow-up appointments in Thunder Bay after her surgery in April 2026.

title: ‘We take care of each other’: Voices from Montreal’s Cabot Square
content:
In Montreal’s Cabot Square, where homeless Indigenous people have gathered for decades, news that a member of the city’s police services (SPVM) had been suspended for urinating on homeless Montrealers was greeted largely without shock.




Regular visitors, as well as outreach workers from the various organizations serving unhoused populations in the west of downtown, describe relations between homeless people and police in and around Cabot Square as marked by distrust and fear.




People APTN News spoke with in Cabot Square over the last two weeks reported accumulating tickets, amounting to hundreds of dollars in fines, for fare evasion on the city’s transit system or jaywalking on Ste. Catherine Street. People who drink alcohol in the Square also said they’d received tickets for open containers. 

Few make any attempt to pay the tickets. For them, getting another ticket is simply a fact of life in Cabot Square, though one that may give police a reason to eventually arrest them.




Cabot Square




Measuring one block by one block, Cabot Square is the only significant piece of greenspace in the western end of downtown Montreal. Located on Ste. Catherine St. at the corner of Atwater Ave., the Square is directly across from the former Montreal Forum.

author: Cierra Bettens
title: InFocus: What’s at stake for Indigenous Peoples in the U.S. as midterm elections draw near?
content:
On Tuesday, U.S. voters will cast their ballots in the country’s midterm elections. The elections come halfway through a president’s four year term.

A record-breaking number of Indigenous candidates–at least 355–are running in this year’s race.

This week on InFocus, Pawnee/Ponca lawyer Brett Chapman tells us about the candidates he’s following and how Native Americans are feeling the impact of Trump’s second term.

A recent study by the Brookings Institution reported that the Trump administration slashed $469 million in grants and contracts to tribal communities.

“I think a big problem with the administration, the second go around, is that because of the focus by them on DEI [Diversity, Equity and Inclusion], things of that nature, they have really tried to reduce Native American issues to [being] race-based,” Chapman said.

“What defines being Native American in the United States is not being a member of a race. It’s political sovereignty in the history of over 500 tribes having treaties with the government, and they’re having their own governments. And so you’re having a government-to-government relationship.

“You’re really seeing a weakening of that when it should be stronger.”

title: N.W.T. premier commits to advancing Dene control of child welfare
content:
Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson says the territorial government will begin discussions with Yellowknives Dene First Nations on formalizing their authority over child and family services, following concerns raised at the Annual Akaitcho Assembly about Indigenous children in care.




Speaking to delegates at the Chief Drygeese Centre on Oct. 28, Simpson said that while Indigenous governments already have the authority to care for their own children, the next step is to begin working toward a coordination agreement between governments under federal legislation.




“In terms of the child welfare piece, we will begin those conversations,” Simpson said. “It’s federal legislation, and it requires an implementation,” said Simpson.




The discussions come as delegates described children being separated from their siblings and communities, families struggling to access services and concerns about whether the child welfare system adequately reflects Indigenous cultures and ways of life.




According to a 2026 federal audit, 98 per cent of children who receive prevention and protection services in the N.W.T. are Indigenous, despite making up only about 58 per cent of the territory’s total child population.

author: Fraser Needham
title: Columnist says more pressing issues on agenda at First Nations meeting than abolishing Indian Act
content:
A columnist with the Hill Times says a First Nations meeting with First Ministers this week was not the appropriate venue to be discussing abolishing the more than a century-and-a-half old Indian Act.

“It seems to me that a lot of things were said at mics on that day that people really regret,” Rose LeMay said. “I don’t know anyone who would disagree that the Indian Act has to go. It’s a racist piece of segregationist law. It always has been. Whether we take out a clause here or there it’s still fundamentally a barrier to human rights. Especially for First Nations women. We’ve seen all the debate on S-2 and trying to bring in the one parent instead of the second-generation cut-off. Overall, it’s a piece of racist legislation. Was that day the day to raise it? I don’t think so.”

Lemay said it is her understanding that much more time in the meeting was spent on discussing how the government’s proposed Bill C-39 – the Building Canada Strong Act – could affect First Nations rights when it comes resource development.

She also said more pressing issues including First Nations access to health care and systemic discrimination against First Nations women should have been given more of a focus by government ministers in post meeting media scrums.

title: Federal government says lack of housing on First Nations ‘strictly’ a funding issue
content:
During the final hour of a two-day hearing at the Federal Court of Appeal, lawyers representing First Nations and Canada argued whether the matter of water and housing on reserve land was about money or human rights.

Canada asserted that when it comes to providing housing, the government “is limited” to providing funding for the homes, making the issue a matter of financial duty.

“First Nations manage their own housing,” said one of Canada’s lawyers. “Leadership determines what is to be built, where it is to be built, and how it will be contained.”

However, lawyers representing Shamattawa and St. Theresa Point First Nations asked how that could be possible, when the Indian Act had caused the housing shortages that are affecting Indigenous communities in the first place.

“There’s such extreme harm that we can say that there’s no way a First Nation would have brought this on itself if it could have afforded it,” said Michael Rosenberg, one of an equally plentiful team of lawyers representing the Nations.

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon photographer captures caribou’s extraordinary fight for survival
content:
It’s an incredible act of nature.




Two caribou. Their antlers locked in battle. One dead. The survivor, nearly immobilized by the weight of his opponent, preyed upon by a bear as foxes and birds scavenge the dead bull’s remains.




Yukon

 photographer 

Peter Mather

 captured the remarkable images earlier this month while filming the Southern Lakes caribou’s rut, when up to a few hundred animals gather and males spar for females.




“I have never seen anything like that before,” Mather said. “Their horns are locked together, and one of them is dead. And the bear is like sitting 10 feet away, just watching, trying to figure out what to do. It was the strangest situation.”




Mather came across the rare sighting about 20 kilometres south of Whitehorse while filming content for the Kwanlin Dün First Nation as part of a project for the Southern Lakes Caribou Steering Committee. Kwanlin Dün is one of six First Nations governments represented on the committee.




With fewer than 1,000 animals in the early 1990s, the Southern Lakes caribou, which is composed of four woodland herds, has increased to about 4,000 today, thanks in part to voluntary harvest moratoriums by First Nations.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: First Nations youth, MP Leah Gazan warn new federal laws threaten rights, water and consent
content:
First Nations youth and NDP Indigenous affairs critic Leah Gazan used a Parliament Hill news conference Wednesday to warn that three major federal bills risk undermining treaty rights, free, prior and informed consent, and protections for water and land.




Gazan was joined by Ramon Kataquapit, who sits on the 

Chiefs of Ontario’s Youth Council

, and other First Nations youth advocates, Jeronimo Kataquapit, Cedar Iahtail, Dara Wawatie-Chabot, Katisha Paul and Celine Debassige. 




They focused on the proposed bills, C-39 (the Building Canada Strong Act), C-37 (the First Nations Clean Water Act), and the Bill C-5, which passed in 2025, arguing the legislation prioritizes rapid resource development over Indigenous jurisdiction and long-term community health.




Gazan said that Bill C-39’s one-year review timelines and expanded ministerial powers to exempt projects from certain environmental and heritage rules effectively hinder Section 35 rights and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

title: Federal drinking water lawsuit ‘not a case of government spending,’ says lawyer
content:
A lawyer representing Shamattawa First Nation says that if Canada is in control of what’s being built on reserve land, then it would also be responsible for addressing the needs related to clean drinking water and housing.

“If you don’t take Canada’s money, the infrastructure does not get built, does not get operated, does not get maintained,” said defense lawyer Michael Rosenburg, during a hearing in the Federal Court of Appeal on Wednesday in Winnipeg. “That is the dynamic, because these First Nations have been put in this position of dependence.”

In December 2025, Federal Court Justice Paul Favel determined that, in his rulings for two separate class-action lawsuits from Shamattawa and St. Theresa First Nations, that Canada had the obligation to provide these communities with access to housing and clean drinking water.

In one of the decisions, Favel said that the federal government “exerted direct control over every facet of First Nations life through legislations, regulations, policies, and practices since at least the 1880s,” and that “this extends to matters such as water infrastructure.”

author: The Canadian Press
title: Youths tell trial of climate change toll, from anxiety to flood and heat impacts
content:
Sadie Vipond says she was just seven years old when she began noticing the impacts of climate change.




Now a 20-year-old plaintiff in Canada’s first youth-led climate trial, Vipond described experiencing catastrophic floods in Calgary in 2013 that the city says resulted in mass evacuations, one death and $6 billion in financial losses.




“I was beginning to see different actions in my community around the climate crisis, and so I was also feeling very anxious about my future,” she told the Federal Court in Vancouver.




Vipond is one of 15 plaintiffs who are arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.




The trial that began Monday heard in an opening statement from the youths’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, that the case is not about the existence of climate change but rather whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse.”




She said the Charter must protect youth from their own government’s actions.




Vipond told the court on Tuesday that she had experienced several climate change events since the floods, including wildfire smoke and intense heat.




“I’ve been seeing these impacts all my life, and I’ve been seeing how these impacts are getting worse,” she said, adding that they had taken a toll on her mental health.

author: Karyn Pugliese
title: Nearly 200 First Nations leaders, the prime minister and premiers gathered for a historic meeting about almost everything. Now what?
content:
The John G. Diefenbaker Building on Sussex Drive was perhaps, in its own imperfect way, a fitting place for nearly 200 First Nations leaders, most of the country’s premiers and a prime minister to hold a meeting First Nations have wanted for more than a century.




It’s actually two buildings mashed together: a modern glass construction, like a church nave, that lets light pour in from above and gives the hallways a sense of something sacred, while behind it, the old city hall rises as a plain grey slab, a maze of stairs leading to small, dark meeting rooms. 




Outside, the chief set up teepees that strangely echo the building’s peaks.




Three very different structures, sharing the same address.




“This is the first time in 119 years of Crown-First Nations relations that a first ministers meeting has focused solely on First Nations,” Cindy Woodhouse-Nepinak, the national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, has said many times leading up to the meeting and it’s a line she would repeat at the gathering.




Of course, a hundred-year wait puts a lot of pressure on a meeting.
